children.text: Capones Island, with a lighthouse built by Spain's colonial government in
, and Camara Island, where a sandbar joins two small islets, make up Zambales' classic island-hopping route by boat from Pundaquit beach. It works as a day trip, and some visitors camp overnight.
Capones Island and Camara Island lie just off Pundaquit, a fishing village in San Antonio, Zambales. Capones is about
4km
from the Pundaquit shore and is a long, bone-shaped island roughly
1.9km
long and
across at its widest. Administratively it belongs to Barangay Pundaquit. Camara sits closer to the coast, so the boat gets there quickly, and it is in effect two small islets joined by a sandbar.

The two islands look quite different. Most of Capones is grass-covered rocky cliff, with small beaches of white sand and coral debris and stretches of rounded boulders tucked in between. The water shifts in layers from deep blue to jade, and from the cliff tops you can see the coral bottom below. Camara is gentler and more intimate, with a low shoreline, a sandy islet with coconut palms, rocky bluffs and an enormous fallen boulder resting on the beach.
The face of Capones is its lighthouse. Spain's colonial government built it to guide ships entering and leaving Subic Bay and Manila Bay, and it was first lit on
August 1, 1890

. It has watched over the west-coast sea lane for more than a century. Today the Coast Guard runs the light on solar-powered equipment, while the old brick keeper's house stands roofless and windowless, swallowed by undergrowth. The government has listed the lighthouse as an Important Cultural Property. There are no shops or electricity on the island and the phone signal is weak, so it still feels cut off from the mainland.

Unlike trips to Anawangin or Nagsasa, where you head for a campsite, these two islands give you history, a sandbar, snorkeling and sunsets in a short boat ride. They suit office workers leaving Manila at dawn for a day trip, photographers, and families and groups of friends who want a light hike and some time in the water. If you have two days, you can combine them with
Anawangin Cove
or
Nagsasa Cove
From the shore where the boat lands, the walk up the grassy ridge to the lighthouse usually takes about
1 hour

. There are no signs and piles of stones serve as trail markers, so follow the route your boatman or a local guide points out. At the top you are surrounded by sea, and on a clear day the mountains of the Zambales coast spread out in view.
Just below the lighthouse stands the old keeper's house, built of brick and plaster and now reduced to its arched window openings. An old photo taken around

, early in the American period, shows the same building with its roof intact, and comparing it with what you see today brings home the weight of the years. The building could collapse, so photograph it from outside only.

The tower today has a white octagonal top with a railing around it, and a solar-powered lamp has replaced the old Fresnel lens. Whether you can climb up depends on conditions on the day, so ask on site. When access is open, the balcony beside the lantern room looks out over blue sea and the green forest of the island.

Heading down the ridge west of the lighthouse brings you to grassland that ends at a sheer drop. When the sun is high, glitter spreads across the water and waves break on the rock pools below the cliff. There is no railing at the edge, so stay two or three steps back.

Camara is two nearby islets joined by a narrow sandbar. Depending on the tide, the sandbar appears or disappears, and when the sea is calm and the water has dropped you can sometimes wade across the shallows. From one side, the palm-covered islet seems to float on the water, which makes this a favorite photo spot.

On one side of the Camara beach, a boulder as big as a house that broke off the cliff leans at an angle on the sand. Its rough surface, studded with rounded stones, is fully exposed. Do not rest in the shade beneath it; admire it from a distance.

The water off the Capones beach is clear, and the bottom is scattered with coral pieces and rocks, so even a mask and snorkel will show you small tropical fish. On days with strong waves it is easy to scrape your feet on the rocks, so wear water shoes. You can borrow life jackets from the boat.

Around sunset, looking out to sea from the Camara beach, you see the sun sink toward the horizon with distant islands layered as silhouettes. If you camp overnight, or take a boat out from a Pundaquit resort in the late afternoon, aim to be here at that hour.

children.text: At Pundaquit beach, find the boat association office, confirm the route and fare, and pay the environmental fee.
Put on life jackets, board the outrigger boat and head for nearby Camara Island.
Swim and take photos on the Camara sandbar while the water is clear in the morning.
Move on to Capones Island, which takes about
20–30 minutes
Land on the pebble shore and climb the ridge toward the lighthouse.
Look around the lighthouse and the ruined keeper's house, then come back down to the beach to snorkel.
Eat the lunch you brought and rest. There is no shade, so you need a hat and an umbrella.
Head back to Pundaquit before the wind picks up.
Take a shower, have a late lunch in San Antonio, then set off for Manila.

items.title: Overnight camping course
items.subtitle: If you spend a night on the island

children.text: There are no shops or lodging on the island, so you must bring your own tent, food, drinking water and trash bags. Ask the Pundaquit boat association or the local office in advance whether camping is allowed and where you may pitch your tent.
Arrive at Pundaquit, load your gear on the boat and stop first at Camara Island to see the sandbar.
Land on Capones, choose a camping spot and pitch your tent.
Once the heat eases, walk up to the lighthouse and enjoy the view in the afternoon light.
Watch the sunset and cook a simple dinner. Make fires only in designated places.
At first light, watch the sunrise and stroll along the rocky shore.
Pack the tents, gather your trash and take the boat back to Pundaquit at the agreed time.

It is about
167km
from Manila to San Antonio. Take NLEX and SCTEX and head toward Subic and Olongapo, and it takes about
4–5 hours
. You can park for a fee at Pundaquit resorts and private homes.
From Clark International Airport (CRK), the airport with direct flights from Korea, it takes about
2–3 hours
by car through Olongapo to San Antonio. By public transport, go from Clark to Olongapo and transfer to a bus bound for Iba.
This stretch of sea is wide open to the South China Sea, so the seasons differ sharply. During the
November–May
dry season rain is rare, the sea is relatively calm so boat rides are easy, and the water is at its clearest.
November–February
is cool and good for walking up to the lighthouse, while
March–May
has warm water that suits swimming and snorkeling, though the midday sun is very strong.
In the
June–October

rainy season the southwest monsoon (habagat) pounds the coast, raising waves and bringing typhoon effects. On many days the Coast Guard or the local government stops small boats from leaving, so trips are easily cancelled. Even in the dry season the wind rises in the afternoon, so it is safest to reach the islands in the morning and leave before noon.
Pundaquit gets very crowded during Holy Week and on weekends of the
March–May
school break. Boats and places run short, so it is better to pick a weekday or
November
or
January–February

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Capones has no lodging, so most people stay at a resort or guesthouse on Pundaquit beach and go out by boat. A room costs roughly

, based on a room for four people. On weekends and during Holy Week they fill up early, so book a month ahead. The advantages are that you are close to the beach for an early boat and can wash up as soon as you return.

Nothing on the islands sells food, so you have to bring your own lunch and snacks. You can buy fish, shrimp and fruit at the San Antonio public market, and Pundaquit resorts can also prepare packed meals on request. Zambales is the home of Philippine mangoes, so do not miss the in-season mangoes in
April–May
It is most efficient to visit Capones and Camara in one go. When renting a boat, first check that the fare covers both islands and whether waiting time is included.
The earlier in the morning you go in, the calmer the sea and the weaker the sun. Plan to be back at Pundaquit before the afternoon wind rises.
There is almost no shade on the way up to the lighthouse. Bring a hat, sunglasses, a long-sleeved rash guard and at least 1.5 liters of water per person.
The shores are mostly pebbles and rock, so water shoes or thick-soled sandals are essential. Flip-flops are slippery.
When you step off the boat onto a rocky shore, the water can reach your knees. Put your camera and phone in a waterproof bag.
You cannot count on a phone signal or charging on the islands. Carry a power bank and cash, and tell your family your plan and return time.
Renting a boat through the boat association or a resort makes it easier to keep to the return time and to have safety equipment. Be sure to get the boatman's phone number.
Take your trash back with you. Bring a large plastic bag and the basic rule is to carry out everything you carried in.

This sea is open to the South China Sea, so waves rise in the afternoon and boats are barred from leaving in the rainy season. Follow any Coast Guard sailing restrictions, and if the boatman says it is dangerous, shorten the trip or cancel it.

The cliff edges have no railings and the sea is directly below. Do not stand at the edge for a photo, and the grass is slippery after rain. Watch out for falling rocks below cliffs, as at the Camara beach.
The roof and walls of the lighthouse keeper's house are broken. Do not enter the building or lean against its walls.
The beaches have no lifeguards and some spots have strong currents. Put life jackets on children and weak swimmers.
At midday with no shade, heatstroke and sunburn come easily. Drink water often and rest around noon.

Whether camping or overnight stays are allowed, and the fees, change from time to time. Before you leave, check the latest notice from the Pundaquit boat association or the San Antonio tourism office.

by boat from Pundaquit. A wider, quieter volcanic-ash beach that suits an overnight trip.
